params.question: A student palpates a horizontal ridge on the sternum to begin counting ribs. Which anatomical feature explains why this ridge is palpable at the level of the second costal cartilage?

answers.text: The second costal cartilage is the thickest of all costal cartilages, producing a palpable bulge

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The palpable ridge is not due to cartilage thickness. It is the sternal angle, formed at the manubriosternal joint where the manubrium meets the body of the sternum.

answers.text: The manubrium and body of the sternum meet at a secondary cartilaginous joint, forming the sternal angle

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The sternal angle (Angle of Louis) is the ridge at the manubriosternal joint. This secondary cartilaginous joint reliably marks the second costal cartilage — the starting point for counting ribs.

answers.text: The first rib inserts directly into the sternal body, creating a bony prominence at this level

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The first rib attaches to the manubrium via its costal cartilage, above the sternal angle. It does not produce the ridge used for rib counting.

answers.text: The xiphoid process projects forward at this level, making the ridge palpable

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The xiphoid process is at the lower end of the sternum, around vertebral level T9–T10 — far below the sternal angle and the second costal cartilage.

overallFeedback.feedback: The sternal angle is formed where the manubrium meets the body of the sternum. This joint creates a palpable ridge at the level of the second costal cartilage — your most reliable starting point for counting ribs.

Correct! The sternal angle is the ridge at the manubriosternal joint, marking the second costal cartilage. It also corresponds to the T4/T5 disc, the tracheal bifurcation, and the boundaries of the aortic arch.

params.question: Thoracic outlet syndrome causes compression of vessels and nerves, yet the compression actually occurs at the thoracic inlet. Which of the following best explains why this region is vulnerable?

answers.text: The thoracic inlet is a narrow, rigid opening crowded with major vessels and nerves, and a cervical rib or fibrous band further reduces the available space

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The thoracic inlet is a small, kidney-shaped opening bounded by T1, the first ribs, and the manubrium. It transmits the trachea, oesophagus, subclavian vessels, and brachial plexus trunks in a confined space. A cervical rib or fibrous band narrows this opening further, compressing the subclavian artery and lower trunk of the brachial plexus.

answers.text: The thoracic inlet is sealed by the diaphragm, which contracts and compresses the structures passing through it

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The diaphragm seals the inferior thoracic aperture (the outlet), not the inlet. The thoracic inlet is an open passageway between the neck and thorax.

answers.text: The floating ribs at the inlet are unusually mobile, allowing them to pinch nearby nerves during arm movements

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Floating ribs (11 and 12) are at the lower thorax near the outlet. The first rib at the inlet is short, broad, and firmly attached — its rigidity is part of why the space is so tight.

answers.text: The inlet is wider than the outlet, so the structures passing through are less supported and shift freely

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The inlet is actually much smaller than the outlet. Its narrow, rigid perimeter is precisely what makes it vulnerable to compression when an extra structure like a cervical rib is present.

overallFeedback.feedback: The thoracic inlet is a small opening crowded with vital structures. A cervical rib or fibrous band further narrows this space, compressing the subclavian artery and lower trunk of the brachial plexus — the classic mechanism of thoracic outlet syndrome.
Correct! The thoracic inlet is a narrow, crowded gateway bounded by T1, the first ribs, and the manubrium. A cervical rib or fibrous band can compress the subclavian artery and brachial plexus here.

interactions.label: The second intercostal nerve gives off the intercostobrachial nerve, which cross

params.question: The second intercostal nerve gives off the intercostobrachial nerve, which crosses the axilla to supply the medial upper arm. Why does this explain referred pain down the left arm during a myocardial infarction?

answers.text: The intercostobrachial nerve directly innervates the pericardium and transmits pain when the heart is ischaemic

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The intercostobrachial nerve is a somatic cutaneous nerve supplying arm skin. The pericardium is innervated by the phrenic nerve (C3–C5). Referred pain is a central convergence phenomenon, not a direct nerve link.

answers.text: Swelling of the heart during infarction physically compresses the intercostobrachial nerve in the axilla

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Referred pain in myocardial infarction is a central nervous system phenomenon — visceral and somatic afferents converge at the same spinal cord segments. It is not caused by physical compression of peripheral nerves.

answers.text: Cardiac pain afferents enter the spinal cord at T1–T4, the same segments as the intercostobrachial nerve, so the brain misinterprets the pain as coming from the arm

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Cardiac visceral afferents travel with sympathetic nerves to spinal cord segments T1–T4. The intercostobrachial nerve arises from T2. Because visceral and somatic afferents converge at the same spinal levels, the brain misinterprets cardiac pain as arising from the T2 somatic territory — the medial upper arm.

answers.text: The intercostobrachial nerve carries motor fibres to the heart that go into spasm during ischaemia, producing arm pain

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The intercostobrachial nerve is a purely somatic sensory nerve supplying skin. It does not carry motor fibres to the heart. Cardiac innervation comes from the cardiac plexus via sympathetic and parasympathetic fibres.

overallFeedback.feedback: Cardiac visceral afferents enter the spinal cord at T1–T4 — the same segments as the intercostobrachial nerve (T2). When these signals converge, the brain misinterprets cardiac pain as coming from the arm — classic referred pain.

Correct! Cardiac pain afferents and the intercostobrachial nerve (T2) share spinal cord segments T1–T4. This convergence causes the brain to misinterpret visceral cardiac pain as somatic pain from the medial upper arm.

params.question: During quiet inspiration, which rib movement is primarily responsible for increasing the anteroposterior (front-to-back) diameter of the chest?

answers.text: Bucket-handle movement of the lower ribs

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The bucket-handle movement involves the lower ribs (7–10) and increases the transverse (side-to-side) diameter, not the anteroposterior diameter.

answers.text: Descent of the diaphragm

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Diaphragmatic descent increases the vertical dimension of the thorax. The anteroposterior diameter is increased by the forward and upward movement of the sternum driven by the upper ribs.

answers.text: Pump-handle movement of the upper ribs

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The pump-handle movement involves the upper ribs (2–6) rotating around a side-to-side axis. As each rib elevates, the sternum moves forward and upward — like a pump handle — increasing the AP diameter.

answers.text: Lateral flaring of the floating ribs

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Floating ribs (11–12) lack anterior attachments and costotransverse joints. They do not contribute significantly to changes in chest diameter during quiet breathing.

overallFeedback.feedback: The pump-handle movement of the upper ribs (2–6) lifts the sternum forward, increasing the AP diameter. The bucket-handle movement of the lower ribs increases the transverse diameter. The diaphragm adds the vertical expansion.

Correct! The pump-handle movement of the upper ribs pushes the sternum forward, increasing the AP diameter. The bucket-handle movement widens the chest laterally, and the diaphragm adds the vertical component.

params.question: A CT scan reveals a mass in the mediastinal compartment that lies directly behind the pericardium. Which of the following structures is most likely to be affected?

answers.text: Thymus gland

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The thymus lies in the superior mediastinum in children. In adults, thymic remnants are found in the anterior mediastinum — in front of the pericardium, not behind it.

answers.text: Superior vena cava

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The superior vena cava lies in the superior mediastinum, above the horizontal plane through the sternal angle. It is not in the compartment behind the pericardium.

answers.text: Heart and its great vessels within the pericardial sac

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The heart and pericardium occupy the middle mediastinum — not behind the pericardium. The question describes a mass posterior to the pericardial sac.

answers.text: Descending thoracic aorta

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The posterior mediastinum lies behind the pericardium and contains the descending thoracic aorta, the oesophagus, the azygos and hemiazygos veins, the thoracic duct, and the sympathetic trunks.

overallFeedback.feedback: The compartment behind the pericardium is the posterior mediastinum. Its major contents include the descending thoracic aorta, the oesophagus, the azygos venous system, and the thoracic duct.
Correct! The posterior mediastinum lies behind the pericardium. It contains the descending aorta, oesophagus, azygos veins, thoracic duct, and sympathetic trunks.

interactions.label: When inserting a chest drain, the needle should be passed just below the upper r

params.question: When inserting a chest drain, the needle should be passed just below the upper rib of the intercostal space to avoid the neurovascular bundle.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is false. The VAN bundle hugs the inferior border of the rib above, sitting in the costal groove. Inserting just below the upper rib would injure the intercostal vessels and nerve. The safe route is just above the lower rib — along the upper border of the rib below.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct! The VAN bundle (vein, artery, nerve) runs in the costal groove along the inferior border of the rib above. Inserting just below the upper rib would go directly into the bundle. The safe approach is just above the lower rib of the space.
